title: What are the rulings of idda (waiting period)?
headline: The four schools agree idda is obligatory after consummation and differ on qurʾ and the pregnant widow

summary.text: The waiting period after divorce or death is fixed in the Quran at three menstrual cycles, three months, delivery, or four months and ten days according to her situation. All four schools treat it as obligatory once the marriage has been consummated, and they differ mainly over what the word qurʾ means and over the pregnant widow.

When Does One Start the Waiting Period (‘Idda) in a Khul’ or Faskh Case?

paragraphs.text: The divorcee remains in waiting for three periods, and it is not lawful for her to conceal what Allah has created in her wombs if she believes in Allah and the Last Day. Those who no longer expect menstruation, if in doubt, have three months, and the same for those who have not menstruated; the pregnant woman's term is until she gives birth. The widow waits four months and ten days, a woman divorced before being touched has no period to count, and divorce is to be pronounced at the start of the waiting period, which is to be counted, and she is not to be turned out of the house.

When the term is nearly over the husband either retains her honourably or releases her, with two witnesses, and she is lodged and maintained according to means, with maintenance continuing for a pregnant woman until delivery. The retention must not be a way of harming her, and her guardians must not block her remarriage once the term is complete. The translation of 2:228 itself notes that qurʾ can mean either menstrual periods or the periods of purity between them.

Subai'a al-Aslamiyya gave birth a few nights after her husband's death; she came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked his permission to marry, and he gave her permission, so she married (Sahih al-Bukhari 5320, graded Sahih). The same report appears in Sunan an-Nasa'i 3506, graded Sahih, and in Sunan al-Darimi 2179 without a grade attached in the source. Umm Salama's version adds that the Prophet ﷺ instructed her to marry.

Ibn Umar divorced his wife during menstruation, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to take her back and wait out a further cycle before divorcing, saying that is the waiting period for which Allah commanded that women be divorced (Sahih Muslim 1471a, graded Sahih). It is also in Sunan an-Nasa'i 3392, graded Sahih, and Muslim 1471e. Ibn Rushd records that the party holding qurʾ to mean purity built its case on this hadith, since the Prophet ﷺ counted the cycles as menstruation followed by purity.

It is not permissible for a Muslim woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn for more than three days, except for her husband, for whom she mourns four months and ten days (Sahih al-Bukhari 5339, graded Sahih). Hafsah's version in Sunan an-Nasa'i 3503 is graded Sahih. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports that no intercourse is to take place with a pregnant woman until she delivers, nor with a non-pregnant one until she has one menstrual cycle (Sunan Abi Dawud 2157: graded Sahih by al-Albani and by Muhammad Muhyi al-Din, Sahih li-ghayrihi by Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut, and Da'if by Zubair Ali Zai); al-Tirmidhi's parallel report is graded Sahih by Shakir and al-Albani and Hasan by Zubair Ali Zai, and al-Tirmidhi notes it is gharib.

Ibn Mas'ud's statement about the order of revelation is a Companion report rather than a prophetic hadith, and its chain is graded Sahih by Abu Ghuddah and al-Albani but Da'if by Zubair Ali Zai. Ibn Abbas held that the pregnant widow waits for the longer of the two terms, and a report reached Ali saying the same, though through a disconnected chain; Ibn Qudama notes that Abu al-Sanabil ibn Ba'kak said this in the Prophet's lifetime and the Prophet ﷺ rejected his view. Ibn Mas'ud took the opposite line: the verse on pregnant women was revealed after the verse on the widow, so once she gives birth she is free to marry.

The Hanafis hold that the aqrāʾ are the menses according to us, against al-Shafi'i's purity, and the term runs as three purities or three months. A pregnancy appearing after the death does not change her term; she counts by months. She waits in the marital home, mourning is required even for the irrevocably divorced woman, and intercourse by shubha during the term generates a second term, and the two interpenetrate.

The Maliki passages consulted do not settle the meaning of qurʾ; Ibn Rushd, writing as a Maliki, sets out both readings and their proofs. On the pregnant widow the Malikis hold delivery, as the majority of the jurists of the regions he reports. A slave widow's term is halved, and she is not pregnant in that case; the missing husband's wife waits four years, then four months and ten days, and the mustahada's term is also addressed.

The Shafi'is hold that qurʾ is the purity enclosed by two bloods, the azhar view, reported from Umar, Ali and Aisha. The pregnant widow's term is delivery. A free woman counts three qurūʾ and a slave woman two; there is no maintenance for a widow even if pregnant, and no mourning for the irrevocably divorced woman.

The Hanbalis hold that qurʾ means menses, the sahih position from Ahmad. The pregnant widow's term is delivery, by the consensus of the scholars of all ages except Ibn Abbas. The cycle in which she was divorced is not counted, by consensus; a slave woman counts two qurūʾ; and a woman whose menses stop for no known cause waits a year, nine months for pregnancy plus three for the term.

Al-Shafi'i is quoted saying that the year-long waiting period for the woman whose menses stopped was Umar's judgment among the Muhajirun and Ansar, and no one rejected it. A marriage contracted during the term is void, and if one spouse dies during the term of a revocable divorce the survivor inherits.

The dispute over qurʾ turns on a word that Arabic uses for both meanings, which is why Ibn Rushd opens his chapter by saying the cause of disagreement is the shared name, and that each side tried to show the Quran uses the word in its own sense. The Hanafis argue that the term exists to clear the womb, which happens by menstruation, so the menses are the count; the Shafi'is argue that what is considered is the transition from purity to blood, and that the hadith of Ibn Umar mentions the purity. Ibn Qudama adds the practical point that counting the cycle in which the divorce fell would shorten the term, which is why all sides exclude it.

A Hanafi term is often described as three months and a Shafi'i term as three cycles, and the Egyptian Dar al-Ifta put a floor on it, holding that a menstruating divorcee is not believed to have completed her term in under sixty days from the divorce. The pregnant widow was reconciled by treating 65:4 as general and later, so that it specifies the four months and ten days of 2:234; that is Ibn Mas'ud's argument, it is the reasoning the Egyptian Dar al-Ifta gives for the majority, and Ibn Abbas himself is reported to have returned to the majority position when it reached him. The Subay'a hadith settled the practice, and the four schools as reported by IslamOnline agree that her term is delivery whether she was divorced or widowed.

The exemption in 33:49 covers only the woman divorced before consummation, not the widow: Dar al-Ifta's fatwa 5402 (1970) holds that a widow whose marriage was contracted but not consummated still waits four months and ten days, because the term is for declaring grief at the loss of the marriage bond, not for clearing the womb; IslamOnline gives the same reasoning, quoting Ibn Taymiyyah that the death term is a sanctuary for the ended contract and a right of the husband. On maintenance, Ibn Rushd records agreement that the revocably divorced woman and the pregnant woman get support and housing under 65:6, with disagreement over the irrevocably divorced woman and the non-pregnant widow; the Shafi'i book states there is no maintenance for a widow even if pregnant, while the Hanafis require mourning from the irrevocably divorced woman and the Shafi'is do not.

Ibn Abidin holds that a widow who conceives after the death keeps the monthly term, while Dar al-Ifta's fatwa 3485 of 14 December 2003, from Ali Jum'a, holds that the pregnant woman's term ends at delivery absolutely, even a moment after the death, provided something of the creation is discernible, and otherwise it does not. On divorce before consummation, the modern fatwas restate 33:49 and give the two purposes of the term, clearing the womb and shielding the previous marriage from an immediate successor. The practical summaries for divorcees, widows, the menopausal and the pregnant follow the same fourfold division, and for a khul' or faskh a Hanafi answer holds that the term begins when the Islamic court, scholarly body or Sharia council finalises the paperwork.
